analysis.one_liner: Makes insurers count drugmaker copay assistance toward patients' out-of-pocket limits during the COVID emergency.
analysis.headline: Referred to three House committees the day it was introduced and never taken up, the bill died without a vote despite 37 cosponsors from both parties.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would block, for the rest of the COVID emergency, a May 2020 federal rule that lets health insurers decide whether drugmaker copay assistance counts toward a patient's annual out-of-pocket limit. It would restore the older rule, under which insurers can leave that assistance out of the math only when a cheaper generic version of the drug exists. The change would last until the first calendar year beginning 12 months after the COVID public health emergency ends. [S2] [S3]
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with chronic conditions — asthma, diabetes, cancer, autoimmune disease — who rely on a drugmaker's copay card to afford a brand-name medicine. Under "accumulator" programs made possible by the 2020 rule, the card's value does not count toward the deductible and out-of-pocket maximum, so a patient can pay thousands of dollars out of pocket even while using the assistance. Under this bill, that assistance would count toward their limit, lowering what they owe during the pandemic. [S2] [S3]

how_it_helps.text: Patients on expensive brand-name drugs would have their manufacturer copay assistance counted toward their annual out-of-pocket limit, ending the practice of "accumulator" programs that leave patients owing thousands even while using assistance.

Insurers could still exclude the assistance from the out-of-pocket math when a cheaper generic version of the drug exists, so the protection is aimed at patients whose condition has no generic alternative.
The relief is timed to the pandemic: it applies to plan years starting on or after January 1, 2020 and lasts until the calendar year beginning 12 months after the COVID public health emergency ends.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and the employers that sponsor group health plans would pay more in claims, because assistance that used to vanish from the out-of-pocket math would now count toward patients' limits. Those higher plan costs can flow into premiums for all enrollees. Brand-name drugmakers also benefit, since copay cards keep patients able to afford — and using — their drugs. [S2] [S3]

drawbacks.text: The fix is temporary. It lapses at the start of the calendar year 12 months after the COVID emergency ends, so patients would be back under the 2020 rule and accumulator programs could resume.

Copay assistance keeps patients on expensive brand-name drugs, and the added plan costs can be spread into premiums for everyone. The bill does soften this: under the restored rule, insurers may still exclude the assistance whenever a generic version of the drug is available.

The bill does not ban accumulator programs outright; it only forces a delay of the 2020 rule during the emergency, so the underlying dispute between insurers and drugmakers over who covers high drug costs is left for another day.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For patients who depend on copay assistance, this delivers real, immediate savings during a public health crisis, and the cost falls on insurers and employers rather than on patients directly. The honest caveats are that the protection expires with the emergency, that copay cards prop up brand-name drug prices, and that higher plan costs ultimately show up in premiums paid by everyone. It is a narrow, well-aimed patch rather than a durable fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, and none of them ever voted on it before Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. A. Donald McEachin introduced the bill on July 16, 2020, joined by Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman (D-NJ) and Rep. Rodney Davis (R-IL).

The same day, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce, Education and Labor, and Ways and Means committees, and to Energy and Commerce's Health Subcommittee — the standard first step that lets committees consider whether to take it up.
No committee ever considered or voted on the bill, and no floor action ever occurred; the record shows no action after the initial referrals through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2021.
It drew 37 cosponsors, 34 of 231 House Democrats and 3 of 197 House Republicans, but that support never translated into a hearing, a markup, or a vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employer plans that use copay accumulator programs came out ahead: the 2020 rule stayed in force, manufacturer assistance still did not count toward patients' out-of-pocket limits, and the added costs stayed with patients on expensive brand-name drugs.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was bipartisan but lopsided — 34 of 231 House Democrats and 3 of 197 House Republicans — and no vote ever occurred, so no true party split on the bill was ever recorded.

industries.note: The 2020 rule let plans decide not to count drugmaker copay assistance toward patients' out-of-pocket limits, shifting drug costs back onto patients. The bill would end that during COVID, raising claims costs for insurers and the employers that sponsor plans.

With assistance counting toward patients' limits, patients can better afford brand-name drugs, which keeps them on the manufacturer's product. On this bill the manufacturers' interest and patients' relief point the same way, though copay cards also prop up brand prices — the restored rule still lets insurers exclude the assistance when a generic exists.

Employer plans would bear higher claims costs once copay assistance counted toward out-of-pocket limits, a cost that can be passed into premiums. Their savings under the 2020 rule came directly out of patients' pockets.
